newsitem.title: CANADA: Ottawa seeks top court ruling on Quebec separation.
newsitem.headline: Ottawa seeks top court ruling on Quebec separation.

text.p: The Canadian government, stung by a near loss in a referendum on Quebec separation last year, has decided to ask the Supreme Court to rule on the legality of any future unilateral declaration of independence, Liberal politicians said on Wednesday.

"I am very happy we have decided to go to the Supreme Court," Member of Parliament Sheila Finestone, a Quebecer who used to be in the federal cabinet, told reporters after a Liberal caucus meeting in Parliament.

The decision, which immediately drew the wrath of French-speaking Quebec separatists, was designed to lay the rules of the game out more clearly well ahead of the heat of any future referendum campaign. The Liberal government has consistently declared that the rule of law must be respected in any struggle for sovereignty.
"The minister of justice (Allan Rock) has taken a decision which I personally support," said Member of Parliament Nick Discepola, also from Quebec. "Nobody is above the law."
Rock told Parliament he would announce his intentions in the coming days.

Michel Gauthier, leader of Parliament's official opposition, the separatist Bloc Quebecois, argued that since the Constitution does not speak about the rules of separation, the Supreme Court has nothing to say. "It's our problem, our future," he told the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. "It's not a problem that concerns the judges of the Supreme Court."
Hammering Prime Minister Jean Chretien later in Parliament, Gauthier said in any case Quebec does not recognize the Canadian constitution.

Separatists came within one percentage point of winning a referendum last Oct. 30. Chretien, himself from Quebec, came under scathing criticism after the close call for appearing to have taken few measures to guard against a split.
It was not yet clear what questions the government would ask the court to decide or what would prevent separatists from proceeding with independence regardless of the ruling.
However, Discepola asked: "If they don't do it legally, with the respect of the constitution, how can they lay claim to international recognition as a country afterwards?"

Ottawa's appeal to the Supreme Court would be separate from Quebec lawyer Guy Bertrand's court battle against separation. The former separatist was mulling whether to continue with his demand before a Quebec Superior Court judge for an injunction against any future sovereignty referendums that would lead to a unilateral declaration of independence.

In a move that sparked outrage in Quebec City, the federal government backed Bertrand's case in court, arguing that the Canadian constitution and the courts should have a role to play in any Quebec secession process. Quebec government lawyers argued that Quebec voters alone can decide their political future through a democratic vote in a referendum.

Under Quebec law the separatist Quebec government cannot hold another sovereignty referendum until after the next Quebec election. That is to be called at the provincial premier's discretion and could be up to three years away.
